lesson_title: One Transaction, Three Witnesses: The Buy-back
hook_text: One buy-back, three different numbers on three statements — and all three are right.
clip_script: A company buys back sixty thousand of its own shares at four rand and ninety cents each. Now watch one transaction appear as three different numbers — and all three are correct. Witness one: the bank. Cash is simple-minded; it only knows what left. Sixty thousand shares at the full price — two hundred and ninety-four thousand rand out. That is the cash flow statement's answer. Witness two: the share capital note. The pot of contributed capital holds four rand thirty per share — the average issue price — so the note can only give back what the pot contains: two hundred and fifty-eight thousand. Witness three: retained income. The sixty cents per share paid above the average is old profit, kept back over the years on those very shares, finally paid out — thirty-six thousand rand. Now the move that saves marks under pressure: capital portion plus premium must equal cash. Two-fifty-eight plus thirty-six is two-ninety-four. Locked. If your three numbers fail that addition, you have caught your own error before the marker does. And the sting that hides in the follow-up: after the buy-back, fewer shares share the same profit, so earnings per share RISES — the company looks stronger without earning a cent more. One transaction. Three witnesses. One three-line check that turns a feared question into banked marks.
visual_style: Three spotlit witness stands — a bank vault, a capital pot, a profit jar — each declaring its number; the three figures slide together into a glowing triangle that snaps shut when the addition locks.
mood: Courtroom-crisp, confident, a wink at the end.
pacing: Three deliberate beats for the three witnesses, quickening into the addition check, sharp sting on the earnings-per-share twist.
call_to_action: Watch the full financial-reporting practice run and walk every task with the marks named step by step.
